title: The Kindness Industrial Complex
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian argues that corporate wellbeing programmes in Britain are solving the wrong problem. He sets out the data: 63 percent of UK employees show at least one burnout characteristic, work-related mental health conditions account for 52 percent of work-related ill health, and wellbeing spending is at a record high at the same time. His central claim is a category error, in that meditation apps and resilience workshops are downstream interventions that help individuals cope with conditions that are structural, namely workload, unpaid overtime, job insecurity and poor management. He goes on to suggest that some programmes are really reputation management, which can be spotted because they measure outputs such as app downloads rather than outcomes such as turnover and absence. Citing Deloitte's return of 4.70 pounds per pound invested in genuine support, he describes what good looks like: audited workloads, managers held accountable for team wellbeing, and psychological safety treated as an organisational design problem.
points: The piece reframes burnout as a structural management problem, showing that the leading causes people report are workload, overtime and fear of redundancy rather than a lack of coping tools.

Karian offers a practical diagnostic: organisations serious about wellbeing track outcomes like turnover, absence and engagement, while those performing for reputation track outputs like downloads and webinar attendance.

He cites Deloitte's estimate of a 4.70 pound return per pound spent to argue that the payoff comes from culture change and management quality, not from support offered after someone is already struggling.
The leadership implication is that managers should be held accountable for the wellbeing outcomes of their teams, not only their financial performance.
He closes with a blunt line that the app is what you do when you have decided not to do the hard thing.
quotes: The fundamental problem with most corporate wellbeing strategies is not that they are insincere. Many are perfectly sincere. The problem is that they are solving the wrong problem.

Individual-level interventions (meditation apps, resilience workshops, employee assistance programmes, mental health first aid training) are designed to help individual people cope better with the conditions they find themselves in.
These are not problems that yield to a breathing exercise. They are problems that require decisions about workload, headcount, job design, and management behaviour.

Organisations that treat wellbeing as a genuine strategic priority measure outcomes: turnover, absence, presenteeism, engagement, the proportion of employees who say they feel genuinely supported. Organisations that treat it as reputation management measure outputs: how many people downloaded the app, how many attended the webinar, how many took advantage of the counselling line.

They audit workloads and hold managers accountable for the wellbeing outcomes of their teams, not just their financial performance. They treat psychological safety as an organisational design problem, not an individual attitude problem.

Restructuring job design, reducing excessive workloads, and holding managers genuinely accountable for how their teams feel are hard, expensive, and uncomfortable. Buying an app subscription is easy, cheap, and generates a positive line in the annual report.
